transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-01 15:30 PST — Duration: 58m. Redwood: Alex Kim, Priya Rao. Foxglove: Marcus Lin, Tanya Ortega, Ethan Cho.

Summary: Short intake to understand Foxglove's anticipated token volumes, latency targets, and whether Hosted, Dedicated or Private (VPC/on-prem) is the right path given compliance and budget. Discussed batching/caching levers, rough per‑token economics, and pilot next steps.

Topics: cost per token thresholds; p50/p95 latency goals; caching/prefix reuse; dedicated commit thresholds; VPC and KMS concerns; benchmark plan.

Action items (recap at end): see metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm alex from Redwood, account lead — quick roll call?
[00:05] Marcus Lin: hey, this is marcus, head of ml at foxglove.
[00:07] Tanya Ortega: tanya, infra/platform.
[00:09] Ethan Cho: ethan, finops — i'll be watching budget and approvals.
[00:11] Priya Rao: priya, solutions engineer, i'll handle the perf and pilot details.

[00:22] Alex Kim: great. goal for today is simple — understand your usage profile and constraints so we can recommend hosted vs dedicated vs private. we'll talk levers — batching, kv cache, quantization — and how those affect per‑token price and latency.

[00:35] Marcus Lin: i'll start with context — we want to add LLM summarization and anomaly explanation into payments ops for customer support and fraud triage. expected traffic is spiky — batch of 10s of requests per minute during normal hours but can spike to hundreds per minute during incidents. average prompt length ~400 tokens in, expecting 1200 tokens of generation on average, some outliers to 4k.

[01:02] Ethan Cho: and for finance, we're looking at a rough budget ceiling of $25k/month initially. we'd consider a dedicated commit if unit economics clearly justify it, but need to see break‑even points.

[01:15] Priya Rao: ok good — that gives us a lot. question — are the prompts high reuse? meaning, do you expect prefixes or repeated system instructions that could be cached?

[01:22] Marcus Lin: yeah, actually a lot of the support summaries share common system prompts and templates. we expect maybe 40% prefix reuse in normal flows, higher for some features.

[01:31] Tanya Ortega: security note — we have PCI adjacency concerns. we're not putting card data into model inputs, but we need VPC peering and customer‑managed KMS for keys. SOC 2 plus a vendor questionnaire is required.

[01:44] Alex Kim: understood. Redwood Private (VPC/on‑prem) or Dedicated with VPC options can meet that — we have KMS integrations and audit logs. we'll share security docs asap.

[01:51] Marcus Lin: good. on latency — our p50 target for support chat features is under 120ms for generation time, p95 ideally under 400ms. during spikes we can tolerate higher but want graceful degradation.

[02:03] Priya Rao: couple quick notes — p50 <120ms is a tight target for 1200 token outputs unless you're on optimized hardware with aggressive batching and KV caching. For hosted we can route to low‑latency nodes and use prefix caching, but to get consistent p50 at that seq length, Dedicated or Private with pinned capacity is the safer path. hosted has variability.

[02:26] Ethan Cho: ok — so tradeoff is cost vs predictability. can you give quick back‑of‑envelope per‑token numbers for hosted vs dedicated?

[02:33] Alex Kim: yes. back‑of‑envelope: hosted model A (open quant) — we list at ~$0.0009 per output token when using our shared pool at typical usage, but that's for on‑demand with no caching. with caching & prefix reuse that can drop 20–40% effective tokens billed. Dedicated has a fixed commit and much lower marginal per‑token; for example a mid‑tier dedicated pool in our pricing sheet equates to roughly $0.00035–$0.0005 per token effective depending on utilization and batch efficiency. those are ballparks — we'll run pilot numbers.

[03:05] Marcus Lin: interesting. at 1200 tokens per request and let's say 2k requests/day average, that's ~4.8M tokens/day or ~144M tokens/month — at $0.0009 that's enormous. so caching and batching are critical.

[03:18] Priya Rao: yes — that math shows why we emphasize caching and batching. with 40% prefix reuse, KV cache can reduce generated tokens billed if you repeatedly generate from similar system prompts. Also batching across concurrent short requests reduces GPU per‑token cost. For your spike pattern, a mix makes sense: hosted for baseline and dedicated reserve for spikes or vice versa — or smart routing where we fallback to a cheaper model variant under heavy load.

[03:46] Tanya Ortega: what about quantization? can we run smaller quantized variants that still meet quality?

[03:51] Priya Rao: definitely — model selection and quantization can reduce cost ~30–60% with often minimal quality hit for summarization. part of the pilot is A/B quality checks between q4 and q8 quantized weights and full fp16. We'll propose a quality pass/fail threshold.

[04:07] Ethan Cho: walk me through a break‑even example. say we do a dedicated commit costing $20k/month — at what volume does that pay off vs hosted?

[04:16] Alex Kim: good question. quick example: if hosted avg cost ends up at $0.0009/token and your dedicated marginal cost is ~$0.0004/token after commit, then the per token savings is $0.0005. To offset a $20k monthly commit the required tokens is 20k / 0.0005 = 40M tokens/month. So if after caches you have >40M billable tokens/month, dedicated might pay off. But you'd also consider SLOs and burst capacity.

[04:49] Marcus Lin: our earlier estimate was 144M tokens/month without cache — with 40% reuse that's ~86.4M billable tokens — so looks like dedicated could make sense. but that's sensitive to sequence length and actual cache hit rate.

[05:03] Priya Rao: exactly — pilot will measure real cache hit and batching efficiency. We'll instrument token accounting to show effective billable tokens vs raw token generation.

[05:12] Alex Kim: another lever is model routing — route non‑critical or longer tail queries to a cheaper quantized variant or to a larger batch window that increases latency but cuts cost. Redwood supports policy routing by latency, cost, or region.

[05:24] Ethan Cho: about burst spikes — what's the model for burst capacity on dedicated? we don't want to pay for 24/7 peak.

[05:31] Priya Rao: Dedicated supports autoscale and burst pools. You pay a base commit for reserved nodes and then a burst overlay at higher marginal rates. That gives predictable baseline and handles incidents. We can size commits to cover typical 95th percentile and rely on burst for rare events.

[05:46] Marcus Lin: security again — can we have logs masked and long‑term audit? we need retention for 90 days for audit, but also don't want raw inputs stored.

[05:55] Alex Kim: yes, Redwood supports audit logs with redaction, retention policies, and customer‑managed KMS for encryption at rest. For Private we offer more control (on‑prem or VPC) if you need air‑gapped storage. We'll attach SOC 2 + KMS doc.

[06:07] Tanya Ortega: network connectivity — does Redwood require egress to public internet? we prefer private peering to avoid routing through the public internet for PII adjacency reasons.

[06:14] Priya Rao: we support VPC peering and private link options with dedicated. For hosted, private networking options are available for enterprise tiers. We'll map the networking choices in the doc pack.

[06:27] Marcus Lin: back to economics — can you explain the impact of batching on latency vs cost?

[06:32] Priya Rao: yes. batching increases throughput efficiency by amortizing kernel launch and attention compute, so per‑token cost drops. But it introduces queuing latency; for interactive features like chat, we target small batch windows (e.g., 10–30ms) to avoid perceptible delay. For asynchronous summary jobs you can batch larger to lower cost. We can also do adaptive batching — short latency window for interactive; larger for lows priority.

[06:56] Ethan Cho: do you have typical batch size and latency trade charts we can look at?

[06:59] Alex Kim: yes, priya will include a batching vs cost chart from our internal benchmarks. it shows diminishing returns after certain batch sizes depending on model and seq len.

[07:10] Priya Rao: and we'll include the impact of KV cache: with high prefix reuse, effective tokens billed drop a lot for repeated system prompts. that also reduces opportunity to batch because repeated requests might be faster due to cache hits, but net cost improves.

[07:25] Marcus Lin: what about fallbacks — if a model is slower or capacity constrained, will Redwood automatically switch? we need graceful degradation.

[07:31] Priya Rao: yes — Redwood supports automatic fallback policies. you can route to a compatible, cheaper model variant or different region. Also can set timeout thresholds and return partial results or call an offline summarizer.

[07:44] Tanya Ortega: we have strict timelines — we want pilot in 2 weeks, and decision on commit in 6 weeks. is that realistic?

[07:49] Alex Kim: pilot week of 11/9 is realistic. Decision in 6 weeks aligns with pilot data and a price/commit proposal. We'll prepare a short pilot plan with goals: measure p50/p95, billable tokens, cache hit rate, and quality delta across q8/q4/fp16.

[08:04] Ethan Cho: on quality — how do you suggest we validate summarization quality? human evals? policy tests?

[08:10] Priya Rao: a mix — automated metrics like ROUGE, token overlap, plus a small human eval panel for edge cases. We'll also support regression alerts in Redwood Optimize for prompt sets.

[08:21] Marcus Lin: fine. also curious about caching semantics — can we cache redactions only, or does KV cache store full prompt fragments?

[08:27] Priya Rao: KV cache holds key/value states for transformer context and is tied to token-level prefixes; it's ephemeral per-request stream but we support persistent prefix caching for repeated instructions. For PII you can apply token‑level redaction before caching. We'll document options.

[08:40] Alex Kim: okay, a few housekeeping items — we'll send an invite for the pilot kickoff, plus a security pack. Priya will share the benchmark template and example pilot config (node counts, batch sizes, model variants). Marcus, you'll share the prompt set and seq distribution. Ethan, you'll confirm budget ceiling and procurement path.

[09:02] Marcus Lin: quick question about SLA — what's typical SLO for Dedicated?

[09:06] Alex Kim: typical Dedicated SLOs are 99.95% uptime and p50/p95 latency commitments depending on selected profile. We'll include sample SLA language in the term sheet.

[09:14] Tanya Ortega: regarding data residency — we need EU region support for a subset of customers. do you have multi‑region support?

[09:20] Priya Rao: yes. Redwood hosts in multiple regions and supports regional routing. For private deployments we can deploy in your region as well.

[09:28] Ethan Cho: Elliot in procurement will want a cost sensitivity analysis — can you provide a few scenarios (low, expected, high) showing monthly cost for hosted vs dedicated with and without caching?

[09:36] Alex Kim: yes we'll prepare a 3‑scenario cost model spreadsheet showing break‑even thresholds and recommended commit levels.

[09:42] Marcus Lin: last technical — how do you instrument token accounting so we can reconcile bills?

[09:46] Priya Rao: we emit token logs per request with breakdowns (input tokens, output tokens, cache hits) linked to request IDs and metadata. Redwood Console has token-level dashboards and raw exports you can ingest into your cost systems.

[09:59] Alex Kim: great. anything else from the Foxglove side?
[10:03] Tanya Ortega: can you include network diagrams for VPC peering options? that's important for our infra team.

[10:07] Priya Rao: yes — we'll add network diagrams for hosted private link, dedicated VPC peering, and private on‑prem hookup.

[10:12] Ethan Cho: on procurement, is there a minimal committed term? we dislike long lock‑ins.

[10:17] Alex Kim: Dedicated typically has 3‑6 month minimums for mid tiers but we can be flexible on pilot contingencies and phased commits. We'll put options in the term sheet.

[10:26] Marcus Lin: ok good. i'm curious about the practical steps in the pilot — what's requested from our side on day 0?

[10:30] Priya Rao: day 0 we need: access for our pilot infra to your sample dataset (anonymized), network allowlist for VPC or IPs, and a small set of truth labels for quality eval. We'll run load tests and capture p50/p95 and cache stats over a few days.

[10:43] Alex Kim: we'll also instrument routing config so we can test routing rules — e.g., interactive queries to low‑latency pool, longer jobs to batch pool.

[10:50] Marcus Lin: good. anything else?

[10:52] Ethan Cho: just one more on billing granularity — monthly invoices? can we get per‑project split?

[10:57] Alex Kim: Redwood supports per‑token billing with project and token tags. We can export per‑project invoices or integrate with your billing system.

[11:06] Priya Rao: ok wrapping up — immediate deliverables: benchmark template, security pack, networking diagrams, pilot config, pricing/commit sheet.

[11:12] Marcus Lin: sounds good. i think that covers the main points. appreciate the clarity on break‑even math.

[11:19] Alex Kim: perfect — we'll follow up by EOD with the docs and a 11/9 pilot kickoff invite. thanks everyone.

[11:26] Tanya Ortega: thanks.
[11:27] Ethan Cho: thanks all.

[11:30] End of meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: auto transcription had some speaker overlaps and mis‑capitalized product names (e.g., 'Redwood Dedi' instead of 'Redwood Dedicated' in a few auto segments). Some numeric values were clarified during the call and confirmed in chat afterwards.

References shared during call: pricing deck (link shared in chat), security pack (to be attached), benchmark template (to be sent).
